To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
IgG auto-antibodies are ubiquitous, unique to an individual, and remarkably stable over the life of the individual, suggesting that they may play an important physiological role.

1) IgG autoantobodies are abundant in human sera, usually numbering in thousands; 2) their number and diversity are influenced by age, sex, and disease; 3) their serum diversity is remarkably stable over time; 4) similar profiles exist in rat, swine, and humans; and 5) the number, diversity, stability, and apparent evolutionary conservaton of these IgG autoantbodies suggest a physiological function that is as yet unrecognized.
IgG auto-antibodies to a broad range of self-antigens are abundant in the serum of healthy individuals.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the physiological function of natural IgG autoantbodies and their relationship to the development of autoimmune disease.

the discovery of new biomarkers and the identification of novel therapeutic targets for human disease, and our findings suggest that the IgG antibody repertoire may be an under-appreciated and under-utilized source of biomarkers and therapeutic targets.
the role of autoantibodies as indicators of disease, the mechanisms of their generation, and their potential utility as therapeutic reagents.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the presence of autoantibodies does not necessarily imply disease, but may be a normal physiological response.
autoantibodies represent the normal physiological immune response to the constant turnover of self-antigens and that the immune system has evolved to produce them.
autoantibodies represent a normal part of the immune repertoire of all humans.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
IgG auto-antibodies are ubiquitous, abundant, and stable and their number is influenced by age, sex, and disease, and we propose that they may be involved in a debris-clearance mechanism.
IgG auto-antibodies are not only ubiquitous in healthy individuals, but are also highly conserved among mammals, and that their presence is influenced by age, sex, and disease.
IgG auto-antibodies have a physiological function that is not yet understood, and that they are an important component of the human immune system.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the IgG autoantiglobulin response is a fundamental feature of the human immune system and should not be considered a sign of pathology.
the presence of self-reactivity in human sera does not necessarily indicate pathology, and should be considered in the context of the overall immune-response profile.
IgG autoimmunity, as currently defined, is a normal physiological feature of the human immune system.
